George, a 68-year-old politician, had always been known for his confidence and charisma. However, everything changed after a life-threatening accident that left him grappling with the aftermath. One fateful afternoon, while driving home from a campaign event, another vehicle collided violently with his car. The impact was catastrophic, and George found himself trapped, the world around him filled with the acrid smell of smoke and the metallic tang of blood. He vividly recalled the moments that followed—screams, the sound of shattering glass, and the eerie silence that enveloped him after the chaos subsided. These snapshots of terror haunted him, replaying in his mind as vivid images that evoked physical pain in the same parts of his body that had been injured. The memory was not just a recollection; it was a sensory experience that threatened to consume him. As these memories surfaced, he would often resort to avoidance strategies, retreating from situations that might trigger the painful recollections, believing that staying away would help him manage the distress.

Since the accident, George's life had become dominated by a set of triggers that spiraled him deeper into a cycle of maladaptive coping strategies. Each time he encountered these triggers, he would find himself overwhelmed, leading him to avoid driving and social gatherings, convinced that staying away would spare him the distress of those painful memories. The smell of alcohol, a common scent in the gatherings he frequented as a politician, would suddenly fill his nostrils, leaving him feeling uncomfortable and exposed. When he encountered images of cars in accidents, his heart raced, and he was transported back to that fateful day. These triggers not only provoked intense memories of the crash but also led him to dwell on what he perceived as his failures. When he encountered these triggers, he would often retreat into avoidance, steering clear of reminders like driving and social events, believing that by doing so, he could shield himself from the overwhelming feelings they stirred. He often found himself ruminating on the belief that he could have done something to prevent the accident, replaying the events in his mind and repeatedly blaming himself for the consequences. This conviction that he was at fault kept the memory of the accident vivid and fresh, as he could not escape the thought that he should have seen it coming, forcing him to relive the trauma in painful detail. This self-blame became a heavy burden, compounding his distress and leading him to avoid driving altogether. What once brought him joy—being behind the wheel—had transformed into a source of paralyzing fear.

George’s negative appraisals of himself intensified in the wake of the accident. He had internalized the belief that the crash had happened because of the kind of person he was, which made him feel as if he was constantly under scrutiny. This harsh self-assessment made every new interaction feel like a potential threat, as he was convinced that others were judging him through the lens of his trauma, which heightened his sense of danger in social situations. His belief that he was fundamentally flawed meant that he walked into rooms already braced for judgment, feeling vulnerable and exposed, which only amplified his anxiety and sense of threat in those interactions. He was convinced that others could see the trauma etched on his face, a visible marker of his perceived inadequacies. This belief stoked his hypervigilance; he felt that he had to be on guard all the time, anticipating danger lurking in the silence. The unusual quiet that sometimes enveloped him would trigger a profound sense of impending doom, compounding his anxiety and leading to sleepless nights where he would awaken, heart pounding, to check whether he was safe. This overwhelming sense of danger made every moment of silence feel like a prelude to disaster, causing memories of the crash to surge back into his consciousness, reinforcing his feelings of vulnerability.
